monte_carlo_oprisk_capital.text: `loss_distribution_approach_lda` answers "what capital do my own loss history and event counts imply?", while `monte_carlo_oprisk_capital` answers "what capital follows from frequency and severity parameters I already have?" The first takes raw data (`annual_event_counts` and `loss_amounts`), fits a Poisson frequency and a lognormal severity itself, then simulates and reads off OpVaR and capital in one call. The second skips the fitting: you supply `frequency_lambda`, `severity_mu` and `severity_sigma` directly. It also reports expected shortfall alongside OpVaR, and it describes the confidence level as lying in [0.90, 0.9999]. Both use the same simulation idea, with capital as OpVaR minus expected loss, and both have `n_years` and `seed` to control the simulation. If you want to fit the pieces separately, `frequency_distribution_fitting` and `severity_distribution_fitting` are the related functions.

explain.text: `loss_distribution_approach_lda` (Loss Distribution Approach LDA) runs the full operational-risk capital pipeline in one call. It takes your historical annual loss-event counts (`annual_event_counts`) and individual loss amounts (`loss_amounts`), fits a Poisson frequency distribution and a lognormal severity distribution, then simulates a compound annual loss distribution. From that simulation it reads the OpVaR at `confidence_level`, which defaults to the Basel AMA level, and reports capital as OpVaR less the mean simulated loss, floored at zero. `n_years` and `seed` only control the Monte Carlo simulation and its reproducibility.

when.text:
`loss_distribution_approach_lda` fits when you want a full operational-risk capital estimate from raw history in a single call:

- You have historical annual loss-event counts and individual loss amounts, and want pyvar to fit a Poisson frequency and a lognormal severity from them.
- You want OpVaR and capital read at a chosen confidence level, with 99.9% (the Basel AMA level) as the default `confidence_level`.
- You prefer one end-to-end pipeline (fit, simulate, read the quantile) over running each step separately.
- You need reproducible runs: `seed` fixes the Monte Carlo draws, and `n_years` sets how many years are simulated.

If you only need the frequency fit, `frequency_distribution_fitting` fits a Poisson frequency distribution to annual loss-event counts.
